newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovaks see import surcharge only as last resort.
newsitem.headline: Slovaks see import surcharge only as last resort.

text.p: Slovakia would reintroduce an import surcharge to ease a widening foreign trade deficit only as a last resort, preferring to use other non-protectionist tools, a senior official said on Tuesday.

Deputy Economics Minister Jan Foltin told Reuters the government was seeking an "active and positive" approach to solve the trade deficit rather than imposing administrative measures such as an import surcharge.
"We are not ruling out an import surcharge, but we would prefer to see other mechanisms supporting exports before seriously considering protectionist measures," he said.
Parliament has approved a series of tools recently aimed at boosting exports, including the creation of the state-run Export-Import Bank and a state Fund for Support of Exports.
Slovakia cancelled a widely-criticised import surcharge at the beginning of the year, after cutting it to 7.5 percent from the original 10 percent last July.
"Re-imposition of an import surcharge is one of the possible tools, currently under consideration, to help us overcome the negative trend in our trade balance," Foltin said.
The government imposed the surcharge in March 1994 to help protect the economy during its transition to a market economy, started after the fall of communism in 1989.
But the measure proved ineffective as Slovakia's foreign trade balance showed a deficit of 5.69 billion crowns in 1995, and accelerated to a 64.54 billion crown shortfall in 1996.
Slovakia posted a 7.06 billion crown foreign trade in January 1997, compared with a 2.13 billion crown deficit in January last year.

The Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) set abolition of the surchage as one of the main conditions for Slovakia's membership in the Paris-based group of the world's richest countries. Slovak officials hope to gain membership by the end of the year.
